text.p: The Bank of England officially declared British interest rates on hold on Wednesday despite signs of a strengthening economy as unemployment hit a 17-year low in July.
In its quarterly inflation report, the central bank announced a pause in the current round of rate rises so it could assess where the key risks for inflation lay.
After four quarter-point rate hikes in as many months, it said the next move in rates need not necessarily be upward.
The Bank's announcement came after news that the number of people out of work had fallen by a larger-than-expected 49,800 in July to 1.55 million, the lowest level since September 1980.
"Monetary policy has now reached a position at which it should be possible to pause in order to assess the direction in which the (inflation) risks are likely to materialize," the Bank said.
The Bank's influential chief economist Mervyn King said it was wrong to assume that rates would resume their upward path after the pause.
"I don't think you can come to that conclusion. We have not decided that the next move in interest rates would be upward and that the only uncertain factor is how long we wait," he told reporters.

The Bank of England had hinted last week that interest rates may have peaked after the latest quarter-point rise to 7 percent. That sent the pound plummeting, and it lost 11 pfennigs against the mark by the end of last week.

The pound's response on Wednesday was more muted. But it fell again, partly reflecting a generally stronger German mark. It stood at 2.8970 in early afternoon trading, compared with 2.9399 marks on Tuesday.
British stock prices also fell in response to the strong employment data, but recovered in later trading as U.S. stocks rallied.

In its report, the Bank of England said prospects for low inflation were bright and the underlying inflation rate, which strips out mortgage interest payments, should hit the government's 2.5 percent target in two years.
The underlying inflation rate edged further above the target in July to 3.0 percent from 2.7 percent in June, but the Bank said the surprise jump did not change its view that inflation was on target.
The Bank also shrugged off the sharp fall in unemployment in July.
"There may have been special reasons for that ...and we are not going to react to one month's data," King said.
The drop in the jobless numbers by nearly 50,000 was well above market forecasts calling for a fall of 31,000. The unemployment rate fell to 5.5 percent from 5.7 percent in June.
Fears that strong economic growth would trigger higher inflation were soothed by figures showing growth in British wages had held steady in June at 4.5 percent.
Analysts said while July's unemployment figures were no great cause for alarm, they contained signs that inflationary pressures were building.
